title: Theory of Computer Science — Module 1
description: 450 MCQs: 310 core questions and 140 worked assignment-style problems from the Module 1 lecture decks and formative assignment solutions.
context: Scope: eight Module 1 lecture decks and the supplied formative assignment solutions. These are study questions based on the source materials, not a prediction of the actual midterm.

The original A–D choice order is displayed by default to match the question and answer PDFs. You can enable choice shuffling. Questions with state tables or scanner rules display those tables before the answers; worked solutions are available after answering.

For worked problems, derive the proof, construction, trace, or calculation before choosing an answer. Regular-expression matches mean whole words unless substring search is explicitly stated; ε is the empty word and ∅ is the empty language.

topics.title: Regular expressions
topics.review: A formal regular expression is a finite description of a language. Its building blocks are ∅, ε, and alphabet symbols; its operations are union, concatenation, and star. In this bank matching means the whole word, unless substring search is explicitly stated. Star binds most tightly, then concatenation, then |.

topics.title: Concatenation
topics.review: Concatenation puts one complete word after another. For languages, RS contains every xy with x in R and y in S. It preserves order, is associative, and need not be commutative. {ε} is an identity; ∅ is an annihilator.

topics.title: Alternation
topics.review: Alternation R|S describes union: a word may belong to either language or both. Union is inclusive, commutative and idempotent. It neither concatenates words nor requires both conditions.

topics.title: Repetition and Kleene star
topics.review: L* consists of zero or more concatenated words from L, and zero repetitions always produce ε. Each repetition may select a different word from L. A maximal run is a block that cannot be extended with the same symbol on either side.

topics.title: Language
topics.review: A language is a set of finite words over an alphabet. It can be empty, finite, or infinite. The language containing one empty word is different from the language containing no words. Membership concerns a word; inclusion compares languages.

topics.title: Alphabet
topics.review: An alphabet Σ is the finite set of allowed atomic symbols. Σ^n contains words of length n, and Σ* contains words of all finite lengths. ε represents zero symbols and is not an ordinary member of the input alphabet.

topics.title: String or word
topics.review: A word is a finite sequence. Its length counts positions; |w|a counts occurrences of a. A substring occupies consecutive positions. A maximal run cannot be extended by the same symbol. Word powers repeat a whole word.

topics.title: Regular language
topics.review: The regular languages are exactly those built from ∅, {ε}, and one-symbol languages by finitely many unions, concatenations and stars. Equivalently, they have a formal regex or a finite automaton. Finite languages are regular; infinite languages may or may not be.

topics.title: Regular-language proofs
topics.review: A regularity proof must describe exactly the target language and justify the construction. For an expression, prove both inclusions. For a machine, explain what each state records and why final states match the requirement. Testing examples supplies evidence, not a proof for all words.

topics.title: Closure properties
topics.review: Regular languages are closed under finite union, concatenation, star, complement relative to a fixed alphabet, intersection, difference and reversal. Closure works forward from regular inputs. It does not usually work backward from a regular result to its ingredients.

topics.title: Nonregular languages
topics.review: To use closure for nonregularity, assume the target is regular and combine it with known regular languages to obtain a known nonregular language. An infinite language is not automatically nonregular. A DFA can count modulo a fixed number; it cannot store arbitrary exact counts for later comparison.

topics.title: DFA
topics.review: A DFA has a finite nonempty state set, one start state, a set of accepting states, an alphabet and a total transition function. It has exactly one next state for each state-symbol pair. Its current state records only the information about the prefix needed for future decisions.

topics.title: Accepts, rejects and recognizes
topics.review: Acceptance is a decision about one complete word. Recognition is the statement that the set of all accepted words is exactly a particular language. Reaching a final state midway does not settle acceptance if unread input remains.

topics.title: State, start state and final state
topics.review: A state records a finite summary of the prefix. The start state describes the empty prefix. A final state means the prefix read so far would be accepted if input ended now. A dead state has no accepting continuation; a sink loops on every symbol and may be final or nonfinal.

topics.title: Symbols and input consumption
topics.review: A DFA transition consumes one alphabet symbol. A label such as 0,1 is shorthand for two separate symbol transitions with the same endpoints. ε consumes none. A multi-symbol edge is not a standard DFA edge unless the printed label names a single declared atomic symbol.

topics.title: Alphabet in a DFA
topics.review: A DFA transition table has one destination for each state and each input symbol. Changing the alphabet changes the universe of words and the required transition entries. Complementation must use a specified common alphabet.

topics.title: Transition function
topics.review: The DFA function δ:Q×Σ→Q handles one symbol. Its extension δ* handles words: δ*(q,ε)=q and δ*(q,wa)=δ(δ*(q,w),a). Tables, diagrams and switch statements can implement the same function.

topics.title: NFA
topics.review: An NFA keeps a set of possible current states. This course permits ε transitions. A word is accepted if at least one path consumes the entire word and finishes in a final state, with ε moves allowed before, between and after symbols. Every DFA is a special case of an NFA.

topics.title: Nondeterminism
topics.review: Nondeterminism is a mathematical possibility relation, not random choice or a probability of success. To simulate it faithfully, track all possible states or systematically explore alternatives. A greedy choice of one branch need not preserve the language.

topics.title: Multiple successor states
topics.review: For an NFA, δ(q,a) is a set, not a list of alternative input symbols. From a current set S, first take the union of all a-successors, then take ε-closure. Duplicate destinations appear only once.

topics.title: Epsilon transitions
topics.review: An ε transition changes state without consuming an input symbol. ε-closure includes zero or more ε moves, so it always includes its starting states. Follow chains and cycles to a fixed point; do not follow labeled symbol edges during closure.

topics.title: Scanner or lexer
topics.review: A scanner converts characters into tokens, skips material designated insignificant by its rules, and reports lexical errors. A parser uses the token stream to analyze grammatical structure. Token patterns and token-selection policies must be stated; whitespace is not universally insignificant.

topics.title: Token and token stream
topics.review: A lexeme is the actual input spelling. A token commonly pairs a token type with a value or spelling. Maximal munch chooses the longest valid prefix at the current position. If equal-length matches remain, a separate priority policy resolves the tie.

topics.title: Switch-based, table-based and generated scanners
topics.review: Switch statements and transition tables are alternative implementations of the same transition function. Either may be handwritten; a generator derives code from token regexes and actions. Robust longest-match scanning remembers the last accepting position and preserves unread lookahead.

topics.title: The equivalence theorem
topics.review: A language is regular exactly when a formal regex describes it, an NFA recognizes it, or a DFA recognizes it. Equivalence concerns accepted words, not identical structure, speed, state count, or a one-to-one correspondence between descriptions.

topics.title: Generalized NFA
topics.review: A GNFA permits whole regular expressions on edges. Traversing an edge consumes a word from that edge language. Parallel alternatives are combined with |, a missing edge denotes ∅, and an ε edge consumes the empty word. Fresh start/final states simplify elimination.

topics.title: Collapsing a GNFA
topics.review: When removing q, replace every remaining i-to-j label by R_ij | R_iq(R_qq)*R_qj, using the labels before that elimination step. The direct alternative, zero loop traversals, and updates with i=j all matter. Different elimination orders may give different equivalent expressions.

topics.title: Subset construction
topics.review: A DFA state represents one ε-closed subset of NFA states. Start from E({q0}), repeatedly compute E(union of symbol successors), and retain every reachable subset. A subset is final when it contains at least one original final state. The empty subset, if reached, is a rejecting sink.

topics.title: Equivalence classes
topics.review: States p and q are equivalent when every suffix w leads from p to a final state exactly when it does from q. One distinguishing suffix disproves equivalence. ε already distinguishes a final state from a nonfinal state. Temporary partition blocks are candidates, not necessarily final equivalence classes.

topics.title: DFA minimization
topics.review: Remove unreachable states, partition into nonempty final and nonfinal blocks, and repeatedly split a block when its states transition into different current blocks on some symbol. Stop at a stable partition. Each block becomes one state; the start block contains q0.

topics.title: Pumping lemma
topics.review: If L is regular, there exists p≥1 such that every w∈L with |w|≥p has some split w=xyz with |xy|≤p, |y|>0, and xy^kz∈L for every k≥0. To refute regularity, choose w after p is given, handle every legal split, and choose a failing k. The lemma is necessary, not sufficient, for regularity.
